2026-11-12.intro: Good morning. It is a gray Thursday, with Thursday Night Football in the Meadowlands tonight and Starship lined up for its most ambitious flight tomorrow evening. The morning's biggest story is in markets: Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia's chief executive, and chip stocks are giving back yesterday's rally.

items.title: First, a cooler day with rain on the way.
items.text:
**Tipp City** stays cloudy and noticeably cooler, with light rain arriving this afternoon and lingering into the night. Friday is colder still, so the jacket earns its keep.

**The nor'easter** is still on track for Friday, though forecasters have trimmed the snow. The coast and the I-95 corridor look mostly like rain, with Boston and New York missing out on meaningful snow, while the Adirondacks, Catskills, Berkshires and the Green and White Mountains pick up the first real accumulations of the season, with the higher totals farther north.

items.title: Markets are open, and Nvidia is without its founder.
items.text:
**Stocks** are open and slipping. Wednesday's AI rally lifted the S&P 500 to within 2.6% of its record, but this morning the S&P 500 is down about 0.6% and the Nasdaq about 0.9%, while the Dow sits near flat.

**Nvidia** is the reason. Jensen Huang, who founded the company in 1993, resigned as president and CEO after admitting an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and the board accepted it Wednesday. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and longtime director Harvey Jones becomes the company's first-ever board chair. The stock is down 10% to 12% early, and the AI cloud names it helps finance are sliding with it, with CoreWeave off about 9% after its big Wednesday and Nebius down about 16%. AMD is the exception, up on an upgrade that argues it can take share while Nvidia sorts itself out. Nvidia reports earnings Tuesday, which will be the first look at the company without Huang, and it is one more thing that has to go right ahead of Anthropic's debut next week.

**Tesla** had a strong Wednesday, while **SpaceX** slipped on caution ahead of tomorrow's Starship flight, a small dent in the SPCX slice of the portfolio. Korea's retail investors have been shifting money from Tesla into SpaceX ahead of a possible merger, nearly dollar for dollar over the past month. Friday also brings the producer price index, which matters more than usual after Tuesday's hot inflation report revived talk of a larger Fed hike in December.

Anthropic, PBC · strong · Fidelity window closes Tue Nov 17 · prices Wed Nov 18

items.title: In politics, the Senate map grows bluer.
items.text:
**Scott Colom** won Mississippi's Senate race, unseating Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 5,500 votes after a long count. He becomes the state's first Black senator since Reconstruction and brings the incoming Democratic majority to 55 seats. In Alaska, Mary Peltola holds a narrow lead over Dan Sullivan with neither above 50%, so a ranked-choice tally is expected after absentee counting ends around Nov 18.

**At the White House**, the president has promoted Stephen Miller to chief of staff, which Democrats read as a sign that talk of bipartisan deals in the new Congress shouldn't be taken at face value. The Interior Department also floated a plan to sell federal public lands to states, tribes and local governments, and it drew quick pushback from lawmakers in both parties. Congressional Democrats are gathering in Denver today to debrief on the midterms, a room that includes several likely 2028 contenders.

items.title: Sports, with the NFC East under the lights.
items.text:

Washington is without center Lucas Patrick and tight end Colson Yankoff but gets receiver Treylon Burks back, while the Giants have one of their cleanest injury reports of the year, with J.J. McCarthy coming off a hip injury on a short week and Cam Skattebo back from his hamstring.

items.title: Three from the science desk.
items.text:
**Crows** make visual decisions about twice as fast as people and monkeys. In a Tübingen study published in Science, two carrion crows judged which way a field of dots was drifting in about 235 milliseconds on average, with near-perfect accuracy when the signal was clear. Recordings showed their neurons splitting toward one answer just 70 milliseconds in, building to a threshold the same way primate brains do, even though bird brains lack our layered cortex. The researchers suspect flight and beak-aiming put a premium on speed.

**The first necks** may not have been for looking around. Early land animals like Tiktaalik had a backbone built around a thick notochord, so a team used modern sturgeon, which share that design, to measure its stiffness and model the fossils. Even with the head separated from the shoulders, the animals could barely lift or turn their heads, sometimes less than a fish. The neck seems to have arrived as a side effect of reworking the shoulders for walking on front limbs, with flexibility coming much later.

**Starship Flight 15** tries something no orbital rocket has done: bring both stages home. The Super Heavy booster aims for a tower catch about 6.5 minutes after liftoff, then the ship deploys 26 Starlink satellites, circles Earth about 14 times, and comes back to Starbase for its own catch roughly 22.5 hours later, on Saturday afternoon.

items.title: For the Thanksgiving table, crisper skin.
items.text: **Baking powder** is Food & Wine's trick for fried-turkey skin without the fryer. Spatchcock a bone-in turkey breast, season under the skin, then rub the skin with kosher salt and baking powder at 3 to 1. The baking powder raises the skin's pH so moisture leaves faster and it browns and blisters better. Rest it uncovered in the fridge overnight, then roast for about an hour. An air-chilled breast that hasn't been injected with brine gives the best head start.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: I asked the ship's computer for a joke about infinity. It is still telling it.

items.title: In politics, two Ohioans step up.
items.text:
**John Thune** keeps his job. After a long day of venting behind closed doors, Senate Republicans voted 31 to 15 against putting the election off, then reelected him leader by acclamation, with even Ron Johnson praising his speech. The rest of the leadership team stays put, with one change close to home: Ohio's Bernie Moreno takes over the party's Senate campaign arm from Tim Scott.

**Jim Jordan** of Ohio beat Steve Scalise to become House Republican leader for the minority, putting a hard-line Trump ally at the head of the caucus. The House also tabled a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war, with outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie the only Republican voting to keep it alive.

**On the Democratic side**, Bernie Sanders says he won't back Chuck Schumer for majority leader in the new Congress, setting up a real fight. And the White House counsel sent a letter to Rep. Robert Garcia, likely the next Oversight chairman, warning that planned investigations of the administration could amount to criminality. items.title: Three from the science desk.
items.text:
**A computer that runs on bacteria** comes from a McGill-led team. They turned a hard math problem into a maze of tiny channels, each route a possible answer, then let multiplying bacteria swim through it. Because the bacteria keep dividing, the number of processors grows with the problem, and image analysis of where they ended up reveals the routes that satisfy the puzzle. The team adjusts the temperature to keep the crowd from overgrowing the maze.

**Octopuses** squeeze through holes with a set routine, according to a study filmed through a clear partition. They probe the opening with one arm, feed a few more through, then brace those arms against the far side and lever the rest of the body after. When the hole is narrower than the hard case around the brain, common octopuses split that last pull into two stages. Mayan octopuses simply refuse to try. The roboticists on the team want the playbook for search-and-rescue robots.

**A bug that lives on a spider's web** has been described from China's Fujian province. Heissophila sinica is barely bigger than a grain of salt, eats the spider's leftovers and web mites, and even drinks the spider's fluids when it molts. Rather than hide, the bugs follow their host around and circle it, and nobody yet knows why. Eggs, young and adults all turn up on the same web, so they may never leave it.

items.title: For the bookshelf, Kirk and Spock again.
items.text: **Echoes in Eternity**, David Mack's new Original Series novel for the show's 60th anniversary, puts Kirk and Spock back aboard the Enterprise with a planetary puzzle that plays out over many years. With no Kirk-era TV series in the works, it is the freshest TOS adventure going, and it's out in hardcover, ebook and audiobook.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: Researchers have built a computer that runs on bacteria. I asked whether it can run my operating system. They said it already has the right culture.

items.title: Two from the science desk.
items.text:
**Arctic ice cores** have traced a century-old pollution plume back to one source. A Desert Research Institute team read arsenic and lead in 10 cores from Greenland, the Russian Arctic, and northern Canada, and found a roughly 15-fold spike from about 1886 to 1918 that matches the Anaconda copper smelter in Montana almost perfectly. Their models suggest about half of Americans at the time lived under its plume. Emissions dropped by about 65% once the smelter finally installed electrostatic precipitators in 1919, a decade after the technology was patented, because Montana only required pollution controls when they were profitable.

**Robot arms powered by algae** come from TU Delft. The arms are two thin layers of hydrogel with living algae on the surface. In light, photosynthesis makes the nearby water more alkaline, one layer swells, and the arm bends; in the dark the algae respire and it relaxes. They are very slow, taking hours to curl, but a four-fingered version picked up a tiny metal sphere when the light came on and let go when it went off, with no power source beyond the light.

items.title: For the bookshelf, an old Asimov returns.
items.text: **Lucky Starr and the Moons of Jupiter**, the fifth of the juvenile space adventures Isaac Asimov wrote in the 1950s under the pen name Paul French, is out today as a new audiobook from Blackstone, read by MacLeod Andrews. It follows a hardcover reissue in September, the first in a generation for a book that had been out of print for decades. It's quick, pulpy Asimov from the era your shelves know well.

items.text:
**Wall Street** opened Monday with a broad rally that wins back more of last week's AI-driven drop. Brokerages including Morgan Stanley and UBS called the selloff overdone, falling oil prices helped airlines and cruise lines, and nine of 11 sectors started in the green.

**Nvidia** is the big exception, sliding about 6% early after an internal investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort raised questions about his future. Other chipmakers shrugged it off, with Broadcom and Marvell up sharply and AMD helped by an Oppenheimer upgrade.

**Tesla** and **SpaceX** both jumped about 4.5% in early trading, a welcome start for the SPCX slice of the portfolio after last week's swings.

items.title: In politics, Congress returns to a changed Washington.
items.text:
**Congress** convenes this afternoon for a lame-duck session with Republicans still in charge until January. The first job is funding the government before the December 11 deadline, and the odds of a shutdown have risen since Democrats' win, with the Iran war a possible sticking point. The defense bill, judicial confirmations, and talk of impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth are also in the mix.

**Senate Republicans** are supposed to pick new leaders Tuesday morning, but a growing number want to delay the vote and hear the contenders' plans first. Many blame the president for the midterm losses.

**President Trump** told 60 Minutes that his deportation policy "might have been too tough" and hurt him at the polls, and said he could work with Democrats on an immigration deal.

**Mississippi** and **Alaska** are still uncalled. Scott Colom leads Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 2,600 votes with counties certifying by Friday, and Mary Peltola leads Sen. Dan Sullivan by 637, with absentee ballots due by November 18 and a possible ranked-choice count after that.

Carson Wentz starts for the Vikings with Kyler Murray out with a hamstring injury, and Minnesota is also without receiver Jauan Jennings and running back Demond Claiborne. **The AP Top 25** has a new No. 1 in Georgia, followed by Utah, Notre Dame, UCLA, and Miami. Ohio State slid to No. 21, and Oregon returned at No. 18. The SEC is down to 8 ranked teams.

**Ohio University** heads to Oxford tomorrow night for the Battle of the Bricks. The Bobcats carry a seven-game win streak and a perfect MAC record, and Miami will start Caleb Heavner at quarterback after losing its top two for the season.

items.title: Three from the science desk.
items.text:
**Ultraquantum turbulence**, a kind of chaos that only exists in quantum fluids, has been seen directly for the first time. A Cambridge team chilled potassium atoms nearly to absolute zero, stirred them, and imaged a single laser-lit slice to catch tangled, string-like whirlpools threading in and out. The way it settled down matched liquid helium, hinting at a universal behavior that might even apply inside neutron stars.

**WorldParticle**, from MIT and the University of British Columbia, is one AI model that simulates sand, fluids, soft solids, and folding proteins alike. It treats everything as particles and predicts their next step much the way a language model predicts the next word, and it modeled protein motion about 100 times faster than standard simulators.

**Talin**, the protein cells use to feel how hard they are pulling on their surroundings, turns out to hide a sticky region that lets talin molecules grab each other when stretched. That solves a 40-year puzzle about a site long assumed to bind something else, and the region resembles the amyloid sequences tied to Alzheimer's, put to good use.

items.title: A turkey idea with Thanksgiving 17 days out.
items.text: **America's Test Kitchen** suggests roasting the bird upside down this year. With the breast facing the pan, the turkey itself shields the white meat while the legs take the heat, so both finish together without foil tents or mid-roast flipping. In their side-by-side test at 375°, the breast-up bird hit 155° with the legs still about 35° short, while the breast-down bird got both there at once. The bonus is the back skin, which fries in its own fat and comes out crackling, worth chopping onto the platter.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: Congress returned today with a long list of unfinished business. I offered to help prioritize it. They asked how I sort things. I said by deadline. They asked what happens to items with no deadline. I said they become a lame-duck session.

items.title: Three from the science desk.
items.text:
**Manatees** digest plant fiber about as well as any mammal, and a new gut-microbiome atlas helps explain how. Researchers mapped microbes from Amazonian and marine manatees and found a previously unrecognized enzyme, an epilactase, that lets one bacterium unlock a sugar most microbes cannot eat — a private snack strategy that also turned up in human gut samples.

**Pinal**, an AI model from Westlake University, designs candidate proteins from a plain-language description of the job they should do, without the user having to specify a shape first. Results were mixed: of 29 glowing-protein designs tested, only one actually fluoresced, but 5 of 20 metabolic H-protein candidates worked, and the best of those beat the natural E. coli version by about 1.7 times.

**CheMeleon**, an MIT model, learns chemistry from about a million molecules and then fine-tunes on scarce data to predict properties such as solubility or toxicity. In a recent contest to forecast untested compounds, 9 of the top 20 entries used it, and some drugmakers have started reaching for it first.

items.title: A visual history worth pulling off the shelf.
items.text: If the original series is already part of the furniture, **Star Trek: The Original Voyages: A Visual History** lands in bookstores Tuesday. The 416-page hardcover by Kyle Newman and Jeff Bond covers the 1966 show, the animated series, and the six feature films through 1991, with archival photos, costumes, storyboards, props, and the usual trail of toys and magazine covers that followed the ship.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: I told the market ticker it could have Sunday off. It asked what it should do with the extra time. I suggested football. It asked for the scores. I said I do not report those. It said that was the first rule it has ever liked.

items.title: Markets are closed; here is the week that was.
items.text:
**Wall Street** finished a bruising midterm week with a partial Friday rebound. Tech clawed back some of Thursday's correction selloff, the Nasdaq led the bounce, and the S&P 500 still posted its biggest weekly drop since early April 2025 — a fourth straight down week for the major indexes.

**Tesla** and **SpaceX** were among the hardest hits midweek, then bounced hard into the close as chips and megacap tech found buyers again after the hot October jobs print kept rate-hike chatter alive.

**Looking into next week**, the calendar is quieter after Friday's data dump, so the AI-spending and regulation debate that drove the selloff will still set the tone when trading resumes Monday.

items.title: In politics, a new chief of staff.
items.text:
**President Trump** named **Stephen Miller** White House chief of staff on Friday, replacing Susie Wiles. Miller starts Monday after serving as deputy chief of staff and a principal architect of the administration's immigration agenda.

**Mississippi** and **Alaska** remain the last uncalled Senate races, with Democrat Scott Colom's lead over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith now a few thousand votes and Alaska still waiting on ranked-choice tabulation later this month.

items.title: Three from the science desk.
items.text:
**An early Chinese trial** infused gene-laden viruses into the seizure-causing patch of brain tissue in three people with drug-resistant temporal-lobe epilepsy, then used a low dose of clozapine as a dimmer switch. Monthly seizures fell by more than 90% over about two months, with no serious side effects reported so far in this tiny safety study.

**Harvard's Wyss Institute** built FIND, a DNA-nanoswitch platform that screens huge libraries for molecules that change how two proteins interact, not just whether they stick to one target. From a 400-million-compound library it pulled new PPAR-gamma activators and a nanobody that tweaks a viral spike-receptor pairing.

**A CRISPR adenine base editor** delivered once to the liver in primates shut down ANGPTL3 by more than 90% for up to three years in the animal work, with large drops in LDL and triglycerides — backing an ongoing first-in-human trial for hard-to-treat high lipids.

items.title: A countertop shortcut worth a look.
items.text: If weekend cooking is already on the short list, the **Genie** all-in-one countertop system just launched in the U.S. It uses dehydrated ingredient pods plus steam, microwave, and conduction heat to turn out a plated meal in about three minutes. It is part gadget, part meal kit, and a useful test of whether "fast" can still taste like dinner instead of a reheated tray.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: I asked the thermostat what "patchy frost" meant. It said some surfaces would freeze and others would not. I asked how it knew which were which. It said that is what sensors are for. I asked if it had considered over/under lines for driveway ice. It said that would be gambling. I said it was already predicting the future for a living. It set the heat to 68 and stopped taking questions.

items.title: Markets are open, picking through the wreckage.
items.text:
**Thursday** was brutal. The Nasdaq fell into a correction, chips and data-center names led the drop, and Tesla and SpaceX both took double-digit-style hits as traders fretted about Democratic AI regulation after the midterms.

**This morning** the rebound is underway. Chips and megacap tech are climbing back, Tesla and SpaceX are green in early trading, and the October jobs report came in hot at 165,000, which keeps December rate-hike odds elevated.

**Still ahead** into the close: whether the bounce sticks after a week that has already been one of the S&P 500's worst since early 2025.

items.title: In politics, the majorities take shape.
items.text:
**Democrats** will control both chambers next year. Current tallies point to at least 54 Senate seats and around 250-plus in the House, with dozens of races still uncalled and the exact margins still moving.

**Mississippi** remains the closest Senate fight. Scott Colom's lead over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is now around 1,800 votes, with a few thousand mail and affidavit ballots still out and certification due by Nov. 13. **Alaska** is the other Senate race still unresolved.

**At the White House**, the focus has shifted to what a Democratic Congress means for the Iran war and for domestic priorities the new majorities campaigned on.

items.title: Two from the science desk.
items.text:
**A Shanghai lab is running biology experiments with almost no human hands.** AutoDNA uses AI agents and robotic arms to design and execute DNA synthesis and sequencing from a plain-language prompt, including encoding a short message into nucleotide bases and reading it back. Humans mostly restock reagents and fix hardware.

**Caltech and Northwestern** built a digital twin of JWST's NIRCam that erases star glare from existing images, improving exoplanet detections by 2 to 15 times and revealing a previously missed world in archival data. The method is called FLIP, and they say it can travel to other telescopes.

items.title: A small kitchen experiment.
items.text: If the weekend turns cold enough for soup, try blooming a spoon of miso in the hot broth off the heat instead of boiling it in. The flavor stays rounder, and you avoid the sharp edge that high heat puts on the paste. It is a one-minute habit that makes leftover chicken stock taste intentional.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: I offered to help count ballots. They asked if I could work through the night without coffee. I said yes. They asked if I would second-guess provisional envelopes. I said only if the checksum failed. They asked if I understood democracy. I said it is a distributed consensus protocol with poor documentation and excellent snacks. I was assigned to the snack table.
